newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Swedish booze battle faces final confrontation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swedish booze battle faces final confrontation.

text.p: The hero of Swedish drinkers, small-town grocer Harry Franzen, plans to build a memorial to the bottle if he wins his fight against the state's monopoly on alcohol sales.

Franzen's two-and-a-half year battle of the booze is reaching a head, with a ruling expected in the next two months on the legality of the unpopular monopoly under which alcohol can be sold only by state-owned stores called Systembolagets.
"I am confident about the court decision but if I win or lose I will still have to fight on as I don't trust the government," a jovial Franzen told Reuters.
"I am going to build a big bottle outside a shop, sell wine from the ground floor and set up a museum about my campaign."

Franzen became Sweden's alcohol officials' public enemy number one on New Year's Eve 1994 -- the day before the country joined the European Union -- when he began selling one-litre packs of wine packs from his store in the southern village of Rostanga.
Rostanga's nearest Systembolaget is 18 km (11.2 miles) away.
"Why should people living in the country have to get in their car or take a bus to buy a bottle of wine? It is unnecessarily costly and it is typical across the whole country," Franzen said.

"Why is it so wrong to sell wine in supermarkets along with food? When people from country villages are forced into the town to buy some wine then they tend to buy their food there too and it is killing village shops and services."
AUTHORITIES KEEP TIGHT REIN ON ALCOHOL

Franzen's defiance of the state monopoly outraged the authorities who keep a tight rein on alcohol sales, tax alcohol heavily and ban any advertisements promoting alcohol -- all for the good of the nation's health.

Adding to the inconvenience of distance, the country's 380 Systembolagets are open only from from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from Monday to Friday and alcohol is kept out of arm's reach, displayed in glass cases and numbered for counter service only.

"At least the Systembolaget has stopped putting bottles in brown paper bags now which used to make you feel like a down-and-out alcoholic," said one Swedish advertising executive who declined to be named.

A recent trial self-service store at Mariestad in southern Sweden found sales rose 30 percent when people could pick their own bottles -- fuelling the state's argument that doing away with Systembolagets would send Swedes reeling into ill health.
Franzen was arrested and charged for his behaviour -- but the Landskrona District Court sought advice from the European Court of Justice on the legality of the monopoly under EU law.

On March 4 this year, Court of Justice Advocate-General Michael Elmer said Sweden's regime of governing spirit sales contradicted the provisions in the EU Treaty and recommended the court find the monopoly violated EU rules.
The court usually follows the Advocate-General's advice.
Christian Groth, spokesman for Sweden's Social Affairs Minister Margot Wallstrom, said the decision was likely to be made in late September or October, after the summer break.
"Everyone will then have to analyse the judgement and then decide what to do," Groth told Reuters.
However Wallstrom has said Sweden will maintain its restrictive policy "no matter what the verdict".
She has hinted about a system of permits, opening the spirits market to a network of specialist retailers only, excluding major food retailers.

She could face fierce public opposition. Franzen has won extensive public support for his campaign, with a poll this year finding two out of every three Swedes want to end state alcohol control. Only beer with an alcohol content of less than 3.5 percent is on sale outside Systembolagets.
Swede's love-hate attitude towards alcohol can be baffling to foreigners.

Traditionally Sweden has been a hard liquor-drinking country, where people tend to drink alcohol once a week to get drunk, but stir in a bit of temperance and the result is a hungover Swede with a guilty conscience.
This guilt can be traced back to the late 19th and early 20th centuries when temperance organisations found broad public support, with calls for a complete ban on alcohol.
From 1917 until 1955 alcohol was rationed with everyone's drinking habits monitored via ration books that had to be handed over to buy booze.

It is hard to judge how serious a problem alcohol poses in Sweden but the Alcohol Policy Commission estimates 300,000 of the country's 8.7 million people drink alcohol to excess, meaning to a point where health and social life suffers.
This year Swedish papers devoted pages to the woes of the Left Party leader Gudrun Schyman who declared herself to be an alcoholic after allegedly embarrassing herself in public.
The whole nation debated the evils of alcohol as Schyman checked herself into a clinic to dry out before returning to the political arena, cured.
A cinema in Alvsborg county, northern Sweden, has started showing anti-alcohol adverts during the commercial break -- to such acclaim the project will be made national.
However given a special occasion, Swedes follow their beers with snapps or vodka chasers and have many drinking songs to accompany the clunk of empty glasses on the table.
Bingeing on alcohol remains a popular pastime among young Swedes who go out to get plastered, often drinking in the streets because of the high prices in bars.
"It is Swedish alcohol politics that drives people to this," said Franzen.
"If the system was more relaxed and prices fairer, you wouldn't get people drinking in parks or sneaking off to the lavatories in restaurants to swig out of a bottle."
